alignment.note: Greek ἐξεπλήσσοντο is a single imperfect passive verb ('they were astonished'); the Peshitta renders this periphrastically with predicate ܬܡܝܗܝܢ ('astonished/marvelling') plus the auxiliary ܗܘܘ ('were'), a standard Syriac construction for past durative states. The Vulgate stupebant matches the Greek single-verb imperfect.

Greek uses article + dative noun (τῇ διδαχῇ); Latin uses the bare ablative doctrina without article (Latin lacking definite articles); Syriac fuses the preposition, noun, and possessive suffix into the single inflected form ܒܝܘܠܦܢܗ ('at his teaching'), incorporating the genitive pronoun that Greek and Latin express separately.

The Greek punctuation (high point ·) and the Vulgate colon both mark a sense pause after 'his teaching'; the Peshitta carries no graphic punctuation here and the pronominal possessive is already absorbed into ܒܝܘܠܦܢܗ, so no separate Syriac token corresponds.

Greek ἦν...διδάσκων is a periphrastic imperfect (auxiliary + present participle); the Vulgate erat...docens mirrors this periphrasis exactly. The Peshitta ܡܠܦ ܗܘܐ likewise uses participle + auxiliary, though it places the participle ܡܠܦ before its auxiliary ܗܘܐ, reversing the Greek/Latin order — a difference of word-order within an equivalent construction.

Greek ἐξουσίαν ἔχων ('having authority') is an abstract noun governed by a participle; the Vulgate potestatem habens replicates this exactly. The Peshitta condenses both into the single agent noun ܡܫܠܛܐ ('one having authority / an authoritative one'), substituting a substantival construction for the Greek noun-plus-participle phrase.

Greek καὶ οὐχ ('and not') and Latin et non are two discrete tokens (conjunction + negator); the Peshitta fuses both into the single proclitic form ܘܠܐ ('and-not'), a normal Syriac orthographic conjunction of the connective waw with the negative particle ܠܐ.

Greek οἱ γραμματεῖς uses article + noun ('the scribes'); the Vulgate scribæ drops the article per Latin usage. The Peshitta ܣܦܪܝܗܘܢ adds a 3rd-person plural possessive suffix ('their scribes'), an explicating expansion not present in the Greek or Latin, identifying the scribes as belonging to the hearers' community.
